# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

# UX audit: Calm Registry

I went through the home page, the intake chat, the registry overview, the review flow and the family share page. I checked them at phone width (375) and on your laptop (1290), using your local data, and read the code for each screen. I didn't change any code or data.

## Fix first: these break trust

**1. Family can see items you haven't reviewed yet.** The share link shows everything except skipped items, so all 25 unreviewed draft items appear on `/r/…`. Someone could buy a gift you were about to skip. The filter at [route.ts:15](app/api/r/[slug]/route.ts:15) should keep only kept items. The overview has the same problem: "25 items, about $1,851" counts items you haven't reviewed as if they're on the list.

**2. Quantities count as one gift.** Glass bottles ×4 or swaddles ×3 get marked "Gifted" as soon as one person buys one. The button says "$44.99 at Target" with nothing about the ×4, so it's unclear whether that's the price for one or for all four. Family needs to see "1 of 4 bought" and be able to mark a partial purchase.

**3. Several taps are instant and can't be undone:**
- "Remove" on the overview deletes the row straight away.
- Keep and Skip in review have no way back to the previous item.
- Tapping an alternative product replaces the chosen one with no selected state, so it looks like the list just reshuffled.

Showing an "Undo" toast after Remove and after each Skip would cover most of this.

## Fix next: friction

**4. Returning users lose the home page.** With 9 registries, the "Your registries" box fills the whole first screen on a phone, and the headline and "Start my registry" are pushed below the fold. Titles get cut off on mobile and repeat ("Our Baby Registry" twice, three "Welcome Baby…"), with no date, item count or progress to tell them apart. Fixes:
- Show 2–3 registries with "See all".
- Add one line under each: "25 items · 0 reviewed · made Oct 7".
- When you have registries, put the primary action on the newest one rather than on "Start".

**5. Part of the laptop sidebar is out of reach.** On the overview at 1290×800, the sticky sidebar is 899px tall, so the "Change your registry" input sits below the screen until you scroll to the very bottom of the item list. A proposed change makes the sidebar taller still. Either let the sidebar scroll on its own, or move "Change your registry" to the top of the right-hand column.

**6. The review start screen doesn't say where to begin.** It lists 10 categories that all say "about 1 min", with no button to start. Add "Start with Sleep" as the main button and keep the list for jumping around. On phones the category rows have no arrow or other sign that you can tap them.

**7. The overview mixes two jobs.** Editing (names, answers, review, share, change box) is stacked above the list on mobile, so the items start around 650px down. The sticky change bar also covers part of each row. When there are still items to review, "Continue review" should be the one clear action, and sharing should wait until the review is done. Sharing a draft is how issue 1 reaches family.

## Polish

- **Edit box placeholder is cut off on mobile.** "We're getting a hand-me-down stroller" shows as "re getting a hand-m". Use something shorter, like "What's changed?".
- **Product names don't fit the placeholder tiles.** When there's no photo, the tile shows the item name, and long ones like "Natural Baby Shampoo and Body Wash" spill past the 72px tile. Alternatives with no photo show an empty dashed box. Both should show a tinted tile with a single letter or category mark.
- **Alternatives are hard to tell apart.** At 375 they cut off to "Puddle Duck Organic …", which looks the same as the chosen product. Show brand and price, and wrap the name.
- **The "why" note is hidden on phones** in the overview rows, even though it's what makes this product different. A one-line clamp would keep it.
- **The intake chat's "…" is a bare ellipsis.** It doesn't tell you anything is loading. Animated dots, or "Thinking about your answers", would read better.
- **Gift links switch straight into a confirm step.** "$27.99 at Target" opens the store in a new tab and also turns the card into "Did you buy it?" right away. When people come back without buying, that prompt looks like they already did something. Show it only when they return to the tab, and word it "Did you buy it at Target?"

## What's working
- Calm, specific copy: "Nothing is built until you say so", and errors that tell you what to do next.
- Tap-to-change answers in the chat.
- Writing a change in plain language and approving it before anything happens.
- No horizontal overflow at the sizes I checked.

If you want me to fix these, I'd do 1–3 first because they affect real gifts, then 4–6.
i thought the pages seemed crowded..what did you think

I agree, though the problem isn't tight spacing. The margins are generous. It's that too many things on each screen look equally important, so nothing leads. The review card and the intake chat feel calm because each shows one thing at a time. The overview, the share page and the home page for returning users don't.

**The registry overview is the most crowded.** The sidebar stacks seven blocks, each a label and a button of the same weight: Edit details, Change answers, Continue review, Share link, the suggestion chips, the voice invite and the change box. On a phone all of that sits above the items. A fixed bar at the bottom (chips, text field, mic, Change) then covers part of each row, so you're always reading around controls.

**Each item row has six lines.** Name and price, product title and store, stars with "Read reviews", the italic reason, and "Remove". With an underlined link or two on every row, a list of 25 items becomes a column of underlines. The rose italic reason is lovely on its own, but it shows up everywhere and stops standing out.

**The share page repeats the same pattern.** Each card has stars, a reviews link, the reason, a price button and "I bought it somewhere else". Relatives just need to see what it is, why it's on the list, and where to buy it.

**Home with saved registries** shows a "Delete" and an "Open" on every row, so nine registries means 18 buttons before the headline.

What I'd do is cut things rather than add space:
- **Overview:**
  - Show one main action based on where you are: "Continue review" until you're done, then "Share link".
  - Fold the details and answers into a single "Registry settings" line.
  - Turn the bottom bar into a single "Change something" button that opens the voice room or a text field.
- **Item rows:** keep name, price and the reason. Move ratings to the review card, where you're actually deciding, and put Remove in a small menu on each row.
- **Share page:** make the stars themselves the link to reviews, and drop the separate "Read reviews" link.
- **Home:** show the two newest registries with "See all", and move Delete into each registry's settings.

Want me to start with the overview? It would make the most difference.

A session-scoped Stop hook is now active with condition: "and the stars really should only show up when youre trying to choose if you keep or skip an item..okay fix the crowded registry overview page". Briefly acknowledge the goal, then immediately start (or continue) working toward it — treat the condition itself as your directive and do not pause to ask the user what to do. The hook will block stopping until the condition holds. It auto-clears once the condition is met — do not tell the user to run `/goal clear` after success; that's only for clearing a goal early.
Got it: star ratings will only appear on the keep-or-skip card, and I'll strip the overview back. Reading the sidebar components first.

The app now has a "My registries" sidebar, and product photos no longer have colored backgrounds. Committed and pushed as `88ec70b`.

**Navigation**
- **On a laptop**, a sidebar on the left has:
  - Calm Registry
  - a **New registry** button
  - a **My registries** list, with the registry you're viewing highlighted
- **Unfinished answers** show in the list as "A new registry, 3 answers so far", with an × to discard them.
- **The collapse button** shrinks the sidebar to a slim strip with each registry's first letter (hover to see the full name). It stays collapsed until you open it again.
- **On a phone**, a top bar has a **My registries** button that opens the same list as a drawer.
- **Hidden** on the family share page and when you're signed out.
- **The "Your registries" box is gone from the home page.** "Start one using answers from…" now lives in each registry's settings as "Start a new registry using these answers".

**Product photos** now sit on white with a thin border everywhere: the overview, the review card, the home page examples and the family page. I also noted this in my memory of your design preferences, so the tinted backgrounds don't come back.

**Checks**
- I tried the sidebar, the collapse button and the phone drawer.
- At 1024 the sidebar made the home page scroll sideways, and I fixed it. Nothing scrolls sideways now on home, overview, review, the question chat or the family page at any width from 320 to 1920.

**Still open:**
- **Duplicate names.** Several local registries share names like "Our Baby Registry", so the list has look-alike entries. Showing a date or item count under each would need a small API change. I can add it if you want.
- **"Calm Registry" appears twice on the question chat page on a laptop**, once in the sidebar and once in that page's own left column. Another session is editing that file right now, so I didn't touch it.
